newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists should learn from Blair, minister says.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists should learn from Blair, minister says.

text.p: A French government minister said on Friday the country's opposition Socialists had yet to understand that their British counterparts had won the election because they had dropped "outmoded precepts" about state control of the economy.
Michel Barnier, European Affairs Minister in the centre-right government, said the Labour Party had won because the British public had had enough of "conservative men and ideas".
Barnier said that in France it was the Socialists who were the conservatives "...because they have not made the changes (to their ideology) that Tony Blair and Labour made.

"The British Labour victory was also because of the intelligence of a man and his party (Tony Blair and Labour) who were smart enough to throw into the Thames certain outmoded precepts about the state having to run the economy and who also made their choice for Europe," Barnier told Radio Monte Carlo.
France's Socialists still believe strongly in government intervention in economic affairs.

"What we also saw in Britain, as in Italy, Spain and certain German regions - and I hope we will see in France at election time in a few weeks - is the defeat of all those who have always said 'it's Brussels' fault', 'it's Maastricht's fault,"' he said.
Barnier was referring to increasing concern among some French Socialist leaders at the rapid pace of European integration, which they saw as being increasingly weighted in favour of big business.
"I have the impression that Tony Blair perfectly understood that his place was in Europe, not next to Europe or behind it, but squarely in front," Barnier said.

"On many topics, the new Labour government will have men who want to play a key role in Europe and make Europe advance. on the social level, on the defence level, and I hope, on the level of security for Europe's citizens," he said.

"It's not Europe which provoked France's budget difficulties, it's not Maastricht or Brussels which provoked the deficit of our social security system, it's the Socialist deficits (when they were in power)," Barnier said.

His words were echoed by the centre-right Rally for the Republic Gaullist party which said Blair's victory should make French Socialists jealous "since it shows the French Socialists are living in the past."
Blair's landslide victory knocked France's own election campaign out of the headlines - and in one case off the front page altogether - in French national newspapers.
The left-of-centre daily Liberation ran a full page profile colour photo of Blair as its cover page with the headline: "The Labour wave."
The centre-right Le Figaro ran a six-column headline reading: "Blair succeeds Major" alongside a photo of a smiling Blair.

The British election was also the main fare on French television and radio, most major stations having sent teams or correspondents to cover the result, mostly from London but also from chosen points around the British Isles.

The Blair photo occupying Liberation's front page was in its latest editions, which went to press once his victory was confirmed, because early editions of the newspaper were more cautious, headlining "Europe awaits Britain."
Liberation's top columnist, Jacques Amalric, wrote: "The wear and tear effect is deadly in politics. Leaders wear away while in office but so do ideologies."

Amalric wrote that John Major "lost whatever credit he still had left by accusing Tony Blair of being a puppet of Germany's Chancellor Helmut Kohl. After the Iron Lady (Margret Thatcher), he (Major) was the marshmallow man."
Le Figaro wrote that the "real victor" of the British election was Mrs Thatcher since her ideas "had proved to be irreversible.
"Labour doesn't even pretend today to want to correct the worst Tory excesses. Tony Blair has promised that all he wants to be is the champion of Thatcherism with a human face."
On Thursday night, Foreign Minister Herve de Charette hailed the Labour victory as a blow for "British Euro-scepticism".

"As chairman of the (centre-right) PPDF I note that after 18 years of government by the Conservatives, British voters have decided to change majority," De Charette said in a statement released only an hour after the first estimates of the election result were released.
"As a European, I congratulate myself on an election which, as a whole, marks a step back for British Euro-scepticism.
"As Foreign Minister, I am ready to pursue and develop Franco-British dialogue and cooperation with the new government.
